record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: How should real-world cross-client differences in federated datasets be characterized across feature-distribution skew, label-distribution skew, concept drift, concept shift, quantity skew, violations of independence, and dataset shift so that realistic non-IID benchmarks and mitigation strategies can be built?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning setting in which K clients, indexed by k = 1, …, K, each hold a local data distribution P_k(x, y) over an input space X and label space Y. Cross-client heterogeneity can be decomposed by writing P_k(x, y) = P_k(y | x) P_k(x) = P_k(x | y) P_k(y) and includes the following phenomena:

1. Feature-distribution skew (covariate shift): P_k(x) varies across k while P_k(y | x) is shared.
2. Label-distribution skew (prior probability shift): P_k(y) varies across k while P_k(x | y) is shared.
3. Concept drift (same label, different features): P_k(x | y) varies across k while P_k(y) is shared.
4. Concept shift (same features, different labels): P_k(y | x) varies across k while P_k(x) is shared.
5. Quantity skew: the number of samples n_k varies substantially across clients.
6. Violations of independence: within a client, samples need not be i.i.d., and across clients the availability or selection of clients may be correlated with their distributions (e.g., temporal, geographic, or device-type correlations).
7. General dataset shift: arbitrary combinations of the above.

Problem. Provide a rigorous, quantitative framework for characterizing real-world cross-client differences in federated datasets that simultaneously captures all seven phenomena above. The framework should:

(a) Define formal, measurable divergence quantities D_i({P_k}) for i = 1, …, 7 that isolate each form of skew (for example, by decomposing a joint heterogeneity measure such as Σ_k (n_k / Σ_j n_j) · KL(P_k ‖ P̄), where P̄ = Σ_k (n_k / Σ_j n_j) P_k, into components attributable to marginals, conditionals, sample sizes, and dependence structure);

(b) Yield procedures for estimating these quantities from finite client samples with provable consistency guarantees;

(c) Induce benchmark-generation protocols whereby, given target values of (D_1, …, D_7), one can synthesize federated partitions of standard centralized datasets that realize those values up to controlled error;

(d) Predict, via theorems relating (D_1, …, D_7) to optimization and generalization behavior, the performance degradation and convergence slowdown of canonical federated algorithms (such as FedAvg) relative to a centralized baseline, and identify which mitigation strategies (personalization, clustered FL, multi-task FL, robust aggregation, data augmentation) are provably effective for each individual skew type.

Construct such a framework, or prove obstructions showing that no single framework can simultaneously satisfy (a)–(d).
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of rigorously characterizing non-IID data across clients in federated learning—covering feature/label skew, concept drift/shift, quantity skew, independence violations, and dataset shift—remains an active open research area. Surveys and follow-up works since 2021 (e.g., works on non-IID FL benchmarks like LEAF, FedScale, NIID-Bench) propose partial taxonomies and synthetic benchmarks but no unified quantitative framework with provable guarantees across all seven categories has been established.

status_evidence.title: Federated Learning on Non-IID Data Silos: An Experimental Study (NIID-Bench)
status_evidence.snippet: We propose NIID-bench and categorize non-IID data settings into label distribution skew, feature distribution skew, and quantity skew, evaluating FL algorithms across them.
status_evidence.claim: Existing benchmarks address only subsets of the heterogeneity taxonomy, indicating no unified framework yet exists.

status_evidence.title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Characterizing cross-client differences remains an open problem in federated learning.
status_evidence.claim: Characterization of non-IID heterogeneity is listed as an open problem.
